title: `cairo_pdf(onefile = TRUE)` bug when drawing marquee grob in masked viewport with `border = NA`
description:
I ran into a bug with `cairo_pdf(onefile = TRUE)` when drawing a marquee grob in a masked viewport with a marquee style with `border = NA` which led to subsequent `grid.newpage()` calls being ignored (i.e. extra pages were silently not being created).

This bug can be worked around by using instead `border = "transparent"`.

Ultimately the bug is in base R and a report with patch was submitted to https://bugs.r-project.org/show_bug.cgi?id=19075

Requirements to trigger the bug:

1. `cairo_pdf(onefile = TRUE)`
2. Draw a `glyphGrob` with 2+ glyphs---not in a `groupGrob()`---inside a masked viewport
3. Then call `grid.newpage()` to make new pages

When you set `border = "transparent"` the internals of {marquee} seem to wrap in a the `glyphGrob()` inside a `groupGrob()` which avoids this bug.

title: Alignment of multi-line text in plot axes
description: I'm currently in the process of switching all the theming specifications and defaults of my codebase over to `{marquee}` for its great and comprehensive functionality. During that, I stumbled upon the unexpected (by me, at least) behaviour described below. I noticed it while working with multi-line text on plot axes, but it could be a more general issue. I really hope to not have missed an obvious solution, but after working through the docs and issues for a good deal of time now, I could not find a working solution. I'm on R v4.5.1 with `{marquee}` v1.2.1. The issue I have occurs with multi-line text in axes of a plot . For example, on a horizontal axis, default behaviour of `{ggplot2}` is to center multi-line text. ``` library(tidyverse) library(marquee) p <- iris |> mutate(Species = paste0(Species, "\n\nlorem ipsum dolor sit amet")) |> ggplot(aes(Species)) + geom_bar() # both lines are centered (as the single line would be) p ``` However, when the same theme is marquefied, alignment switches to left-align. ``` # both lines are left-aligned p + marquefy_theme(theme_gray()) ``` From the docs I understand that the preferred way to adjust this would be via the `style` argument in `element_marquee()`. However, changing the alignment style on the `axis.text` level has no effect; centering is only applied when I target the `axis.text.x` specifically. ``` # specifiyng the alignment makes no difference... p + marquefy_theme(theme_gray()) + theme( axis.text = element_marquee( colour = "red", # to test that it does apply this change style = classic_style( align = "center" ) ) ) ``` ``` # ...unless done on the specific axis p + marquefy_theme(theme_gray()) + theme( axis.text.x = element_marquee( colour = "red", # to test that it does apply this change style = classic_style( align = "center" ) ) ) ``` Ultimately, my question is: shouldn't a specification for `axis.text` overwrite a blank value for `axis.text.x`, etc.? Some further tests of variants look to me as if maybe `marquefy_theme()` sets values on some granularity level that then cannot be overwritten by a more general specification that is later applied. Is this the intended behaviour? ``` # example of applying a targeted `element_marquee()`, not marquefying the theme p + theme( axis.text = element_marquee( colour = "red", # to test that it does apply this change style = classic_style( align = "center" ) ) ) ``` This is what I would have expected the plot to look like even if `marquefy_theme(theme_gray())` had been called before the subsequent `theme()` adjustment. Again, I'm sorry if I'm missing something obvious here, I might be blind from all the digging into debugging. 😅

title: Table "margins"
description: I observe that for small tables that their default "margins" can be quite big. I speculate that it may perhaps be possible to calculate better "aspect ratios" for such tables so they aren't so big by default. ```r library(marquee) library(grid) library(gt) table <- data.frame( Rank = c("one per suit", "all eight"), J = c("40", "400"), Q = c("60", "600"), K = c("80", "800"), A = c("100", "1,000") ) table <- gt::gt(table) |> gt::tab_options(table.align = "left") md_text_table <- " * Item 1 * Item 2 ![](table) * Item 3 * Item 4 " style <- classic_style() grob <- marquee_grob(md_text_table, style) grid.newpage() grid.draw(grob) ``` I observe that if your marquee grob has at most one img or table you can manually adjust the table's margins by modifying the `img_asp` style: ```r style <- classic_style() |> modify_style("img", marquee::style(img_asp = 8.0)) grob <- marquee_grob(md_text_table, style) grid.newpage() grid.draw(grob) ``` I couldn't figure a way to individually adjust a table's margins if there is more than one img or table in the marquee grob. This is perhaps to be expected since marquee doesn't yet seem to support custom tags for blocks so it may not yet be possible to separately style each table: https://github.com/r-lib/marquee/issues/3

title: Simplify creation of style sets with defaults
description:
I think the most common use case for style sets in practice is one where we want to use something like classic style but add a few customizations. This is a bit cumbersome with the current functions. See reprex:

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(marquee)

colors <- c(setosa = '#93263E', virginica = '#3947A4', versicolor = '#C6A634')

# set up styling
iris_styles <- classic_style() |>
  modify_style("setosa", style(color = colors["setosa"])) |>
  modify_style("virginica", style(color = colors["virginica"])) |>
  modify_style("versicolor", style(color = colors["versicolor"]))

ggplot(iris) +
  geom_point(aes(Sepal.Length, Sepal.Width, color = Species)) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = colors,
    guide = guide_marquee("{.setosa *I. setosa*} - {.versicolor *I. versicolor*} - {.virginica *I. virginica*}")
  )
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/az4Atjm.png)<!-- -->

I see at least three options to simplify this, not mutually exclusive.

### 1. Add a function `modify_style_set()`

This function would work similarly to `modify_style()` but enable modification of multiple styles at once. Something like this:

```r
iris_styles <- classic_style() |>
  modify_style_set(
    setosa = style(color = colors["setosa"]),
    virginica = style(color = colors["virginica"]),
    versicolor = style(color = colors["versicolor"])
  )
```

### 2. Create style sets with default

This would modify the `style_set()` function to enable a default option.

```r
iris_styles <- style_set(
  setosa = style(color = colors["setosa"]),
  virginica = style(color = colors["virginica"]),
  versicolor = style(color = colors["versicolor"]),
  .defaults = classic_style()
)
```

### 3. Provide an option to update/merge style sets

A function `update_style_set()` could work similarly to `ggplot2:::defaults()`, but with the order of arguments reversed.

```r
custom_styles <- style_set(
  setosa = style(color = colors["setosa"]),
  virginica = style(color = colors["virginica"]),
  versicolor = style(color = colors["versicolor"]),
)

iris_styles <- update_style_set(classic_style(), custom_styles)
```

I'm happy to put in some work to implement this. My suggestion is to start with option 3 and then use it to implement option 1. I'm less sure about option 2 and would leave that aside for now.

title: HTML entities are incorrectly encoded
description:
I believe all the HTML entities defined here: https://github.com/r-lib/marquee/blob/main/src/named_entities.h are incorrect. They all have an extra 0 in the hex representation.

Examples:

` ` defined here:
https://github.com/r-lib/marquee/blob/1a40124b1104fc3d2c76875a4e97e348c4f22fb8/src/named_entities.h#L1399

It should be `\u00A0` but it is `\u000A0`. We can see that marquee returns the latter (with the extra zero).
``` r
cat(marquee::marquee_parse("- -")$text[2]) # marquee result
#> -
#> 0-
cat("-\u000A0-") # same code printed directly
#> -
#> 0-
cat("-\u00A0-") # correct code for non-breaking space
#> - -
```

Another example, `>` defined here:
https://github.com/r-lib/marquee/blob/1a40124b1104fc3d2c76875a4e97e348c4f22fb8/src/named_entities.h#L1077

``` r
cat(marquee::marquee_parse("->-")$text[2]) # marquee result
#> -E-
cat("-\u0003E-") # same code printed directly
#> -E-
cat("-\u003E-") # correct code for > sign
#> ->-
```

It looks to me like the extra 0 is there consistently throughout the entire lookup table, but I haven't checked systematically. Happy to prepare a PR that removes these zeros, as my first contribution to marquee.

title: some examples of how to scale images in marquee
description:
Hi Thomas, thank you for creating marquee. It has expanded the world of possibilities for plotting images and plots inside of plots, so it is very exciting to explore. Teun started a pull request for a new ggrepel function that uses marquee, so I had to spend some time trying to learn how to use it. I hope it is ok that I am creating an issue here to document what I have learned. ---

I wrote these examples in the hope that others would find them helpful.

The main goal of this series of examples is to try multiple ways of changing the size of an image that is included in a geom_marquee() grob.

It seems that omitting width fails to render the image (Example 1) when written like "![]()". However, if we specify width, the image is rendered (Example 4) and we can scale the image (Example 4) by using different values for width.

In contrast, omitting width is OK when we render an image written like "{.p ![]()}" (Example 2), but then the image cannot be scaled (Example 3) with the width argument. Instead of scaling the image, the width argument is scaling the container that holds the image.

Teun showed me that we can scale an image written like "{.p ![]()}" by writing it like this: "{.30 {.p ![]()}}" where 30 indicates some width (Example 3).

In Example 5, I try to compare the width argument to the {.150 {.p ![]()}} syntax. I find that the .150 syntax is not equivalent to unit(150, "points"), so I’m not sure what units 150 is expressing.

I hope this helps others to explore and understand how to use marquee!

If you have more tips, please feel free to share them here.

library(ggplot2)
library(marquee)

Example 1

Should this work? Or is the failure expected?

d <- data.frame(x = 1, y = 1, label = "![](https://cran.r-project.org/Rlogo.svg)")
ggplot(d) + geom_marquee(aes(x = x, y = y, label = label))
#> Error in grid.Call.graphics(C_raster, x$raster, x$x, x$y, x$width, x$height, : Empty raster

Example 2

This seems to fix Example 1, but I don’t know if it is the best approach.

d <- data.frame(x = 1, y = 1, label = "{.p ![](https://cran.r-project.org/Rlogo.svg) }")
ggplot(d) + geom_marquee(aes(x = x, y = y, label = label))

Example 3

Can we modify Example 2 to make the logo larger by using the width argument?

d <- data.frame(x = 1, y = 1, label = "{.p ![](https://cran.r-project.org/Rlogo.svg) }")
ggplot(d) + geom_marquee(aes(x = x, y = y, label = label), width = unit(5, "cm"))

Nope, the logo is the same size, but now it is offset to the left because the width argument scaled the container size instead of scaling the image size..

But wait, what if we use the clever trick that Teun shared ({.30 {.p ![]()}})?

d <- data.frame(x = 1, y = 1, label = "{.30 {.p ![](https://cran.r-project.org/Rlogo.svg) }}")
ggplot(d) + geom_marquee(aes(x = x, y = y, label = label))

Cool! The {.30 {.p ![]()}} syntax works for scaling an image.

Example 4

Surprisingly, it seems that when we provide a width, Example 1 works!

d <- data.frame(x = 1, y = 1, label = "![](https://cran.r-project.org/Rlogo.svg)")
ggplot(d) + geom_marquee(aes(x = x, y = y, label = label), width = unit(5, "cm"))

And we can scale it as large as we want:

d <- data.frame(x = 1, y = 1, label = "![](https://cran.r-project.org/Rlogo.svg)")
ggplot(d) + geom_marquee(aes(x = x, y = y, label = label), width = unit(25, "cm"))

We can scale the image to fit the width of the plot with unit(1, "npc"):

d <- data.frame(x = 1, y = 1, label = "![](https://cran.r-project.org/Rlogo.svg)")
ggplot(d) + geom_marquee(aes(x = x, y = y, label = label), width = unit(1, "npc"))

Example 5

I’m not sure what the number indicates in the {.150 {.p ![]()}} syntax, so let’s see if it is equivalent to using width = unit(150, "points"):

d <- data.frame(x = 1, y = 1, label = "{.150 {.p ![](https://cran.r-project.org/Rlogo.svg) }}")
ggplot(d) + geom_marquee(aes(x = x, y = y, label = label)) +
  labs(title = '{.150 {.p ![]() }}')


d <- data.frame(x = 1, y = 1, label = "![](https://cran.r-project.org/Rlogo.svg)")
ggplot(d) + geom_marquee(aes(x = x, y = y, label = label), width = unit(150, "points")) +
  labs(title = 'width = unit(150, "points")')

title: How to avoid blank first page in PDF output
description: This may be a basic question - I've been here before (blank first page in PDF output) and it's usually something I did wrong. (Related to #43) It appears that `marquee_grob(..., width=NA)` requires an open graphics device, and will open one if needed. I can't figure out a workaround. Example: ```R test_style <- marquee::classic_style( margin=marquee::trbl(marquee::em(0)), padding=marquee::trbl(marquee::em(0.25)), base_size=14, align="center", background="gold", border_radius=4, border_size=marquee::trbl(2), border="red4") pdf("testmarqueegrob.pdf") mg2 <- marquee::marquee_grob( x=0.5, y=0.5, width=NA, hjust="center-ink", vjust="center-ink", text="Test string \n**multiple lines**", style=test_style) grid::grid.newpage() grid::grid.draw(mg2) dev.off(); ``` Aside: I tested with [coolbutuseless/devout](https://github.com/coolbutuseless/devout) to see what was happening at each step. I used the `debug_function` example. Here are the behaviors I observed: 1. If no device is open, `marquee_grob(..., width=NA)` opens a new graphics device. 2. If a device is open, and with nothing drawn, `marquee_grob(..., width=NA)` causes a `'newPage'`. As a result, calling `grid::grid.newpage()` then `grid::grid.draw()` puts the grobs on page 2. 3. If a device is open, with something drawn already. `marquee_grob(..., width=NA)` does *not* trigger `'newPage'`. I never considered that `dev.cur()` would tell me if a device is open, but *not* if it also has a page open. Is it possible to query for "page open"? The same happens if using `png("Rplots%03d.png")`, or running non-interactive R session. it will trigger blank `'test001.png'` when creating the `marquee_grob(..., width=NA)`, then draw the real figure on `'test002.png'`. So, my questions: 1. Is it possible to create a `marquee_grob(..., width=NA)` without requiring a graphics device? If not, then I don't think grobs can be stored independent of plotting. Maybe that's the answer. 2. Is it possible to create the grobs within a null graphics device? Something like `pdf(NULL)`? I noticed that using 'devout' worked: I created the grob within 'devout' then used `grid.draw()` to a PDF later. Will things go wrong with coordinates and res/dpi? 3. Is there another approach? I'm assembling a few grobs together using a gtable, and found that I need to set `width=NA` to make that work. Thank you!

title: Incompatibility between legendry and element_marquee() when using nested labels in legends
description:
Thank you very much for developing and maintaining the excellent package.

I’m reporting a issue I encountered when combining multi-level (nested) labels with element_marquee().
When element_marquee() is applied to axis labels, it works perfectly even with nested labels. However, applying the same style to legend text results in an error. 

Since the error itself arises from marquee, I am reporting it here. However, I’m not entirely sure whether the appropriate solution lies within marquee or legendry, so my apologies if this should be addressed in the other repository.

Below is a reproducible example :

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = F)
library(marquee)
library(legendry)

# Create sample data and nested labels for y-axis
df <- data.frame(
  group = c("A", "A", "B", "C"),
  species = c("species1", "species2", "species3", "species4"),
  abundance = c(10, 15, 20, 5)
) |>
  mutate(
    label = paste0("***", species, "***", "_", "**", group, "**")
  )

# element_marquee works fine on axis text
ggplot(df, aes(abundance, label, fill = species)) +
  geom_col() +
  guides(
    y = guide_axis_nested(
      key = key_range_auto(sep = "_")
    )
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_marquee()
  ) +
  labs(y = NULL)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/OIhPrAU.png)<!-- -->

``` r

# Rebuild nested label for legend display
df <- df |>
  mutate(
    label = paste0("**", group, "**", "_", "***", species, "***")
  )

# Generate plot using grouped legend keys
p <- ggplot(df, aes(abundance, species, fill = label)) +
  geom_col() +
  guides(
    fill = guide_legend_group(
      key = key_group_split(sep = "_")
    )
  ) +
  labs(y = NULL)

# Applying element_marquee() to legend text triggers error
p +
  theme(
    legend.title = element_marquee(),
    legend.text = element_marquee()
  ) 
#> Error in `marquee_parse()`:
#> ! `text` must be a character vector, not a <factor> object.

# As a workaround, ggtext::element_markdown() works fine
p +
  theme(
    legend.title = ggtext::element_markdown(),
    legend.text = ggtext::element_markdown()
  ) +
  labs(y = NULL)
```

title: geom_marquee() and element_marquee() render text incorrectly — all characters are forced to the same height - and width?
description: `geom_marquee()` and `element_marquee()` render all characters — including letters, numbers, and punctuation — with the same height (and possibly also width), regardless of the actual font metrics. As a result, characters lose the distinctive proportions, curvature, and overshoot (and maybe kerning as well) built into the typeface. In comparison, `both geom_text()` and `element_text()` from `base` as well as `geom_richtext()` and `element_markdown()` from `{ggtext}` preserve character shape and alignment correctly. The following code compares `{marquee}` and `{ggtext}`. Notice the differences in the heights of the letters and numerals in the .svg output between the two packages. The total width of the strings are also different with the `{marquee}` string being a little longer, so I suspect `{marquee}` also renders the width incorrectly. ``` library(ggplot2) library(marquee) library(ggtext) library(svglite) library(systemfonts) label <- "Sample text (0123456789)" ggplot() + geom_marquee( aes(x = 0, y = 1, label = label), size = 10, family = "Open Sans" ) + geom_richtext( aes(x = 0, y = 0, label = label), size = 10, family = "Open Sans", fill = NA, label.color = NA, label.padding = unit(rep(0, 4), "pt") ) + theme_void() ggsave("marquee-vs-richtext.svg", device = svglite) ``` **Illustrations from a vector graphics editor** **`marquee()`** Notice how the 7, 8, and 9 are all aligned in the top and bottom, and the parenthesis are aligned with all three of them at the top. **`marquee()`** Notice how the bottom of the S, a, and m are all perfectly aligned at the baseline. **`ggtext()`** Notice how the 8 and 9 overshoot the 7 (at both top and bottom) and the parenthesis (at the top). **`ggtext()`** Notice how the bottom of the S and the bowl of the a overshoots the spur of the a and the bottom of the m (baseline).

description:
Following up on @teunbrand's replies to my https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues/6554 (also maybe @bbcuffer's #79), I get incorrectly-positioned axis titles (or incorrectly-computed plot boundaries) when using `marquee::element_marquee()` to automatically wrap the axis title:

``` r
library( ggplot2 )

plt <- ggplot( data.frame( x=c(1:4), y=c(1:4) ), 
               mapping = aes(x=x, y=y) ) + 
    geom_point()

print( plt + 
           xlab( "A really really really really really really long, just truly amazingly long and crazy incredibly dull x-axis title" ) + 
           theme( plot.background = element_rect( color = "blue" ),
                  axis.title.x = 
                      marquee::element_marquee( vjust=0.5, 
                                                margin=margin(0,0,0,0),
                                                width = 1 ) ) )
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/bAnDH3U.png)<!-- -->

<sup>Created on 2025-08-22 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

Using ggtext's `element_text()` in place of `element_marquee()` yields the same problems, and @teunbrand's comments from the ggplot2 issue post indicate the bug's essentially in the underlying grid graphics-construction algorithm (about which I have basically no knowledge), so I'm fine with closing the issue itself as "not planned".

But given that auto-wrapping axis-titles seems like a very common need (and use case for `element_marquee()`), and that this just doesn't reliably work properly with the current versions of marquee (or ggtext), ggplot2, and R; would it be sensible to include a note in the marquee documentation about this? title: Feature request: text outlines/stroke
description:
Hi Thomas,

I think it is technically feasible to implement text strokes, which could be a worthwhile addition.
The basic idea is that you can use a `strokeGrob()` underneath the text. 

``` r
library(marquee)
library(grid)

txt <- "{.white Here be *italic*} {.red text}."

mq <- marquee_grob(txt, x = 0.5, y = 0.5, hjust = 0.5, width = NA, style = classic_style(16))
stroke <- strokeGrob(mq, gp = gpar(lwd = 2))

grid.newpage()
grid.draw(stroke)
grid.draw(mq)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/bBCwR5s.png)<!-- -->

<sup>Created on 2025-03-22 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

I imagine this being applicable to spans of text, rather than the entirety of the grob.
An additional complication would be (semi)transparent text. Because the centerline of the stroking will go through the font path, the interior will also be inked, which looks bad. I'm sure there can be a creative solution to this too.

title: Bottom margin in "label_style"

The [docs for geom_marquee](https://github.com/r-lib/marquee/blob/be5737856c9f6d560e40e10906d5f6ba5a132658/man/geom_marquee.Rd#L158C1-L167C82) show how to mimic `geom_label()` with marquee. Now, I am not sure if this is the intended behavior, and anyway it goes away by setting the margin for `p` elements to zero, but, after seeing #23, I was wondering whether this might be due to the fact that the margin is not collapsed properly.  So I have two questions:
* Assuming that most people would prefer no margins around their labels, would it make sense to add `margin = trbl(0)` to the `label_style` in docs linked above?
* Are you considering collapsing or removing the margins when there is only one element (or for the last element in the document)?

title: Document NA width
description: OMG I found a solution in #4 ! Yay. Oh joy it works! I have two suggestions for your help docs: 1. For `marquee_grob()`, you might add a sentende to `width` with something like: "Use NA to set the grob width based upon the rendered text, helpful when applying a fill or border." (Sorry I'm not sure how best to describe it.) 2. For `basic_style()`, I suggest distinguishing padding and margins, something like: "Note: margins refers to the margin between successive paragraphs, padding refers to the regions around the entire text box." For example, I set margins to em(0) to remove the whitespace between paragraphs, very helpful for a multi-line label. I made a little test case as a visual, so I'm going to show it. Haha. (If there is a better way to put a box around the text, I'm happy to hear it.) ```R test_string <- "Test string\n\n**multiple lines**" # custom style with border test_style <- marquee::classic_style( padding=marquee::trbl(marquee::em(0.25)), margin=marquee::trbl(marquee::em(0)), base_size=14, align="center", background="gold", border_radius=4, border_size=marquee::trbl(2), border="red4") marquee_grob1 <- marquee::marquee_grob( x=0.5, y=0.6, default.units="npc", name="test_marquee", text=paste0(test_string, "\n\nwidth=NULL"), hjust="center-ink", vjust="center-ink", style=test_style) grid::grid.newpage(); grid::grid.draw(marquee_grob1); marquee_grob2 <- marquee::marquee_grob( x=0.5, y=0.4, default.units="npc", name="test_marquee", width=NA, text=paste0(test_string, "\n\nwidth=NA"), hjust="center-ink", vjust="center-ink", style=test_style) grid::grid.draw(marquee_grob2); ``` Output looks something like this: (For clarity, I was trying to get the bottom solution, with a box matching the text region.)

title: `element_marquee()` does not use font families created with `register_font()`
description:
When a style uses a font family created using  `systemfonts::register_font()`, that font is not picked up in text elements in ggplot2 created using `element_marquee()` - see first plot in reprex below. When the same font file is used directly by referring to the family found in the system font list, it is used correctly in the text element - see second plot. At the same time, plain ggplot2 does pick up the family name created via `register_font()` - see third plot. 

Reprex below was created on MacOS but the same occurs on Ubuntu.

The workaround is to install the fonts on the system, but that is much less convenient and not always feasible.

title: Set default's `element_marquee()`'s margin to 0?
description:
Hi Thomas,

I've been playing around a bit and found it surprising that `element_marquee()` comes with a default (bottom) margin.
I'm aware that `element_marquee(margin)` gets funneled to `style(padding)`, so the only reasonable way to remove it is to edit the style.

For example, if you have tiny keys, `element_text()` legend text is tightly packed:

``` r
library(ggplot2)
library(marquee)

p <- ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, colour = class)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme(legend.key.size = unit(0, "cm"))

p
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/1qeijc9.png)<!-- -->

However, if you use `element_marquee()` there is a large bottom margin. At first I was confused because I thought it was the `vjust` that was off, but it turned out it is the margin.

``` r
p + theme(legend.text = element_marquee())
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/gXVSo4m.png)<!-- -->

My proposal is to let the `element_grob.element_marquee()` adjust elements where `style = NULL` to discard the bottom margin, so that `style(padding)` is the only determinant of the spacing around the text.

``` r
p + theme(legend.text = element_marquee(
  style = classic_style() |> modify_style("base", margin = trbl(0))
))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/GSBoH9M.png)<!-- -->

<sup>Created on 2024-06-01 with [reprex v2.1.0](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

Happy to submit a PR if you agree.

title: Implement `xDetails` / `yDetails` methods?
description:
Hi Thomas,

I know it is early days for marquee, but could I ask that the `xDetails()` and `yDetails()` grid methods be implemented for marquee grobs? It is not of a very high priority.

The main reason I'm asking is because it might allow integration with {ggrepel}, which I think would be exciting.
I've an open PR (https://github.com/slowkow/ggrepel/pull/249) that allows one to swap out the grob generating function, but the `grobX()` and `grobY()` functions, which are fed by the `xDetails()`/`yDetails()` methods should give reasonable coordinates for it to work.

Basically, what one would like these functions to do is to give the coordinates of the bounding box given an angle `theta` in degrees.
For `textGrob()` this works as follows:

``` r
library(grid)
library(marquee)

theta <- seq(0, 315, by = 15)

label <- "Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur 
adipiscing elit. In hendrerit metus quam, 
sed rutrum nulla feugiat consequat. Sed eu 
pulvinar purus, vel placerat metus."

txt <- textGrob(label, rot = 45)

grid.newpage()
grid.draw(txt)

x <- grobX(txt, theta)
y <- grobY(txt, theta)

grid.points(x = x, y = y, gp = gpar(col = 'red'))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/45L7Sqh.png)<!-- -->

For `marquee_grob()`, it just yields central points.

``` r
mq <- marquee_grob(
  label, classic_style(), 
  angle = 45, x = 0.5, y = 0.5, hjust = 0.5, vjust = 0.5
)

grid.newpage()
grid.draw(mq)

x <- grobX(mq, theta)
y <- grobY(mq, theta)

grid.points(x = x, y = y, gp = gpar(col = 'red'))
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/gOyjOwx.png)<!-- -->

<sup>Created on 2024-04-30 with [reprex v2.1.0](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

I imagine the easiest way is to calculate the 4 corner points of the bounding box of the grob and then use something like the following to reuse the `xDetails.points` method:

```r
xDetails.marquee_grob <- function(x, theta) {
  
  #...
  # calculate 4 corner bounds of bounding box
  #...
  
  pts <- structure(
    list(
      x = unit.c(x1, x2, x3, x4), 
      y = unit.c(y1, y2, y3, y4)
    ), 
    class = "points"
  )
  xDetails(pts, theta)
}
```
